topic: lime plastering on riven laths: haired coarse stuff, keying, curing damp and the finish coat

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: higrometr powieszony przy oknie na czas wiazania. UWAGA: mundane_type zmieniony ze 'procesowy' (zlecenie) na 'konkretny', bo inaczej balans EN wychodzi 23/25 i walidator odrzuca caly katalog

base: I am replastering a back bedroom in lime over riven laths and my first coat has cracked badly.
The old ceiling in the hall is original lime work and has not moved in a hundred years.
A hygrometer hangs by the window so that I can watch the room while the work dries.
I mixed putty and sharp sand at one to three and laid it on rather thickly.
Was the coat too thick, or should I have put hair into the mix as well?
Hair, certainly, because a coarse coat on laths without hair has nothing holding it together.
Ox hair or goat hair, a good handful to the bucket, beaten well into the wet mix.
The hair binds the nibs that squeeze between the laths and keeps them from breaking off.
Half an inch is thick enough for a first coat, and anything thicker cracks as it shrinks.
I beat goat hair into the next batch and laid it thinner across the whole ceiling.
The hygrometer showed the room at forty per cent, which seemed quite dry to me.
The coat went off very fast and the surface has dusted where I scratched the key.
Should I be damping the room down, or was the mix simply too lean in lime?
Damp the room down, since lime that dries before it sets never gains any strength at all.
Forty per cent is far too dry, and you want the room nearer seventy while it cures.
Hang wet sheets, close the window and mist the work morning and evening for a week.
Dusting is the mark of a coat that lost its water rather than one short of lime.
Wet sheets and misting brought the room up and the second coat has cured hard.
I scratched the key with a lath comb and left it a fortnight before floating.
The old ceiling has a key just like that where a patch has fallen away in the corner.
My float coat has come up slightly hollow in two places about a foot across.
Should those be cut out now, or will the finish coat bridge over them safely?
Cut them out now, because a hollow under the float will always find its way through.
Tap the whole ceiling with your knuckles and mark every dull sounding patch with chalk.
Cut back to sound work, wet the edges well and make good with the very same mix.
Let the repairs stand a full week before you float over the whole surface again.
Bridging a hollow only moves the failure to the finish coat, where it shows far worse.
I cut out both hollows and made good and the float coat now rings sound everywhere.
The finish coat is next and I have fine putty and silver sand ready for it.
I have read that the finish should be laid on in two passes rather than one.
Is that so, and how long should I leave between the first and the second?
Two passes, and the second follows the first as soon as the surface will take it.
That is usually within the hour, when the sheen has gone but the coat still gives.
Lay the first thin and true, then close the second with a steel trowel and water brush.
Trowel it up three times over the following hours and the surface will polish itself.
The finish went on in two passes and I trowelled it up three times as you said.
It has been on the ceiling for a month and is still faintly grey in patches.
The old ceiling in the hall is a warm white and has been so for generations.
Will mine come round to that colour, or have I done something wrong with the putty?
It will come round, and grey patches at a month simply mean the lime is still curing.
Lime takes carbon from the air slowly, working inward from the surface over many months.
A ceiling of that thickness whitens through the first year and settles in the second.
Leave it bare or use a limewash only, because anything tight will trap what is still working.
